reason: The DAX page states API-compatible with DynamoDB and only minimal functional changes, and the usage notes list Go, Java, Node.js, Python and .NET with AWS-provided clients.
The quote states that writing large amounts of data through DAX invokes LRU eviction and diminishes DAX as a read cache.

The quote applies to the scenario where the item was written through DAX and is still in the DAX item cache, then updated directly in DynamoDB; the claim drops that condition and reads as if any direct update causes inconsistency.
Item cache section: on a miss DAX sends the request to DynamoDB, which uses eventually consistent reads; DAX stores the items in the item cache and returns them.
The Warning in DAX access control says the use of DAX can subvert IAM policies that restrict access to DynamoDB table data.
The document history row, dated October 30, 2025, announces DAX PrivateLink support in commercial and China Regions for private connectivity to DAX control plane endpoints within the same Region.
The document history row dated April 29, 2025 states added support for r7i instance types in DAX, expanding instance type options.
The quote states the DAX client directs all DynamoDB API requests to the cluster; DAX processes what it can and passes the rest through to DynamoDB.
The quote says it is possible for two clients to read the same key from the same DAX cluster and get different values depending on the node, while an update replicates.
The quote states you must associate the cluster with an IAM role at creation, known as the service role.
Constraints page, DAX Nodes: exactly one primary node and between zero and ten read replica nodes.
DAX cluster components states up to 11 nodes per cluster, the primary plus a maximum of 10 read replicas.
Under When not to use DAX, compliance requirements: DAX does not currently offer the same accreditations as DynamoDB and has not obtained SOC yet.
The quote says with a high cache hit rate the reduced table read cost can exceed a DAX cluster cost, a net cost reduction.
Configuring TTL settings lists the item cache and query cache, says the default TTL for each is 5 minutes, and says a custom parameter group sets different TTLs.
The quote states data persisted by DAX on disk is encrypted with 256-bit AES under encryption at rest.
The Note states a new DAX cluster with encryption at rest enabled uses an AWS managed key to encrypt data at rest.
The DAX encryption at rest Note says customer-specified AWS KMS keys are not supported.
The quote states encryption in transit cannot be enabled on an existing DAX cluster.
The quote states clusters with encryption in transit do not support unencrypted traffic, so no chance to bypass encryption.
Use cases section states eventually consistent data with microsecond latency and that a Multi-AZ cluster can serve millions of requests per second.
The FAQ on extra cost options lists DAX, a DynamoDB-compatible caching service that reduces latency through in-memory cache, in a partial list of options that can be added.
The FAQ says for response times in microseconds DynamoDB integrates with DAX, a fully managed, highly available caching service built for DynamoDB.

The FAQ states DAX delivers up to a 10 times performance improvement, from milliseconds to microseconds, even at millions of requests per second, and describes it as fully managed and highly available.
The Important note states one-node and two-node clusters are not fault-tolerant and AWS does not recommend fewer than three nodes for production.
The quote states that to allow access to a DAX cluster you must include DAX-specific actions in an IAM policy.
Use cases list both application types as ideal for DAX, and the surrounding text gives the one-day sale hot-key example.
The quote says DAX is a write-through caching service designed to simplify adding a cache to DynamoDB tables.
Item cache section states results of GetItem and BatchGetItem are stored and represent eventually consistent data from DynamoDB.
The quote states you must create a new cluster with the new node type to use a larger node type.
The quote only says the overhead of maintaining the cache might not justify the gains for infrequently read data; the claim turns this into the definite conclusion that DAX is not worth it.
Item cache section: if the item cache becomes full, DAX evicts older items even if not expired to make room for new items.
Simple applications bullet says DAX might not be necessary and DynamoDB alone handles high throughput with single-digit millisecond performance.
The quote states negative cache entries in both caches and that DAX caches an empty result instead of generating an error.
The quote states DAX does not automatically refresh its item cache in response to updates through DynamoDB.
The DAX product page says no need to manage cache invalidation, data population or cluster management, and no application logic modification is required.
Other operations section: DAX does not recognize table-management operations such as CreateTable and UpdateTable; the application must access DynamoDB directly.
The quote, about an UpdateItem through DAX replicating to other nodes, states replication is eventually consistent and usually takes less than one second.
Constraints, DAX Nodes: the total number of nodes per AWS account cannot exceed 50 in a single AWS Region.
The list of applications for which DAX is not ideal includes those that do not require microsecond reads or do not need to offload repeated read activity.
The not-ideal list names strongly consistent reads, write-intensive applications and applications without many repeated reads, and states DAX performs best when cache hit rates exceed 90%.
Constraints, DAX Parameter groups: you can create up to 20 DAX parameter groups per Region.
The quote states DAX passes strongly consistent reads to DynamoDB, does not cache the results, and cannot serve them by itself.
The pricing example for a three-node t2.small DAX cluster states $0.12 per hour ($0.04 x 3 nodes).
The DAX product page says that, similar to DynamoDB, you only pay for the capacity you provision.
A cluster has one or more nodes; one is the primary and additional nodes, if present, serve as read replicas.
The PrivateLink page says it covers DAX management APIs, that DAX interface endpoints only support management API access within the same Region, and that you are charged for the interface endpoint.
The Important note states three nodes are required for a DAX cluster to be fault-tolerant and that one- and two-node clusters are for development or test.
Query cache section: stores results of Query and Scan as result sets stored by their parameter values.
The quote states a zero query cache TTL means the query response will not be cached.
The High availability bullet states DAX automatically fails over to a read replica and designates it as the new primary after a primary failure.
The quote states DAX is designed to run within an Amazon VPC environment.
The quote states a DAX cluster in a Region can only interact with DynamoDB tables in the same Region.
Nodes section: adding more nodes to the cluster increases the overall read throughput.
Security groups section: an ingress rule specifies TCP port 8111 for the cluster so applications in the VPC can access it.
The quote recommends additional DAX clusters with an IAM policy scoped to each cluster if you require isolation.
The service role policy defines the DynamoDB actions the cluster can perform on behalf of the users who interact with it.
The Important note says do not place all nodes in a single Availability Zone because the cluster becomes unavailable if that AZ fails.
The Higher read throughput bullet says a partition starts throttling reads of an item at 3,000 RCU and DAX lets you scale single-item reads beyond that.
The sizing guide states that with a DAX cluster the DynamoDB ConsumedReadCapacityUnits metric only accounts for cache misses.
Estimating cache hit rate: typical hit rates for applications using DAX are 85-95 percent; the page also notes rates vary by application and TTL.
Constraints, DAX Subnet groups: up to 50 DAX subnet groups per Region.
Constraints, DAX Subnet groups: within a subnet group you can define up to 20 subnets.
The quote states TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems are both supported in DAX with the same isolation levels as DynamoDB.
Constraints, DAX: a cluster supports a maximum of 500 DynamoDB tables; beyond that availability and performance may degrade.
The quote states that with or without encryption in transit, traffic between the application and the DAX cluster remains in your VPC.
The quote states TransactGetItems calls pass through DAX without caching, the same as strongly consistent read APIs in DAX.
The quote states DAX calls TransactGetItems in the background for each item to populate the cache, consuming additional read capacity units.
The quote states users inherit the permissions of the DAX cluster's IAM policy when they access that cluster.
Under complex querying needs, the page says to use ElastiCache (Redis OSS) as an alternative, which supports advanced data structures such as lists, sets and hashes.
The quote states that for write-latency-sensitive applications you can reduce latency by writing directly to DynamoDB; the context names this write-around.
Write-heavy workloads bullet: the primary advantage of DAX is speeding up reads, and for predominantly write-heavy applications DAX benefits might be limited.
Write operations section lists BatchWriteItem, UpdateItem, DeleteItem and PutItem: written first to the table then to DAX, successful only if both succeed.
The quote states writing through DAX incurs an extra network hop for latency-sensitive applications.
The Throughput default quotas table row Per account shows On-Demand not applicable, Provisioned 80,000 RCU and 80,000 WCU, Adjustable yes.
The quote states adaptive capacity is enabled automatically for every table at no additional cost and needs no explicit enable or disable.
The Note states adaptive capacity applies to on-demand mode and provisioned capacity.
The quote states adaptive capacity lets the application keep reading and writing hot partitions unthrottled provided traffic does not exceed total provisioned capacity or the partition maximum.
The quote states adaptive capacity works by automatically and instantly increasing throughput capacity for partitions that receive more traffic.
Isolate frequently accessed items: adaptive capacity rebalances partitions so frequently accessed items do not reside on the same partition.
